issues.legal_issue: Participants in a sudden fight are not vicariously liable for one another’s acts when the evidence does not establish a common object that makes their assembly unlawful.
material_facts: The parties initially exchanged remonstrances, and neither side attacked the other at the outset.
The fight began suddenly, without premeditation, and the evidence did not establish which side struck the first blow.
The other participants wielded their blunt weapons after the fight had begun and the opposing party was seen to be armed.
The courts below found no facts establishing that the participants shared an object falling within the grounds for an unlawful assembly.
issues.conclusion: The participants did not form an unlawful assembly, including for the purpose of enforcing a right by criminal force. They were liable for their individual acts, not vicariously for the acts of others; the convictions based on unlawful-assembly liability were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 141 of the Indian Penal Code, an assembly is unlawful only if its members share one of the specified common objects; clause (4) requires a common object to enforce a right or supposed right by criminal force or its show. Section 149 does not impose vicarious liability where the required unlawful common object is not established. The Court cited no earlier cases.

rule.if: appeal_from_group_assault_convictions and sudden_unpremeditated_fight and no_assault_at_initial_confrontation and no_proven_unlawful_common_object

predicates.appeal_from_group_assault_convictions: The matter is an appeal challenging convictions arising from an alleged group assault.
predicates.sudden_unpremeditated_fight: The parties became involved in a fight that arose suddenly and without premeditation.
predicates.no_assault_at_initial_confrontation: Neither side attacked the other when the parties first confronted one another.
predicates.no_proven_unlawful_common_object: The evidence does not establish that the participants shared an object that made their assembly unlawful.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns group-assault convictions and the fight was sudden, began without an initial attack, and involved no proven unlawful common object, collective liability is not imposed.

issues.legal_issue: A participant who personally inflicts a fatal wound remains individually liable for that act even when the other participants are not vicariously liable for it.
material_facts: One participant personally thrust a spear into the victim’s abdomen.
The wound was fatal, and the victim died from the resulting injuries.
The assault occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation.
issues.conclusion: The conviction of the participant who inflicted the fatal wound under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code was maintained, and the Court held that the sentence was not excessive.
issues.legal_principle: Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code applied to the participant’s own fatal act. The absence of an unlawful common object precluded vicarious liability for others’ acts but did not displace liability for an act personally committed. The Court cited no earlier cases.

predicates.appeal_from_homicide_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a homicide conviction arising from a group altercation.
predicates.accused_personally_inflicted_fatal_wound: The accused personally inflicted a wound that was fatal.
predicates.fatal_wound_caused_death: The fatal wound caused the victim’s death.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a homicide conviction and the accused personally inflicted the wound that caused death, the individual homicide conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A participant whose proven individual act caused simple hurt cannot be convicted for a more serious injury when the evidence does not identify that participant as its cause.
material_facts: Four participants caused simple hurt with blunt weapons.
One grievous injury was caused by a blunt weapon, but the evidence did not establish which participant caused it.
The other participants’ convictions for offences beyond simple hurt depended on attributing injuries to the group.
issues.conclusion: The four participants were convicted only of the offence of causing simple hurt under section 323 of the Indian Penal Code; their other convictions were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 323 of the Indian Penal Code supported conviction for the simple hurt proved to have been caused individually. A more serious injury could not be attributed to a particular participant where the evidence did not identify its cause; section 149 could not supply collective liability in the absence of an unlawful common object. The Court cited no earlier cases.

rule.if: appeal_from_group_assault_convictions and individual_simple_hurt_proven and grievous_injury_occurred and actor_for_grievous_injury_unidentified

predicates.appeal_from_group_assault_convictions: The matter is an appeal challenging convictions arising from an alleged group assault.
predicates.individual_simple_hurt_proven: The evidence establishes that the accused personally caused simple hurt.
predicates.grievous_injury_occurred: A grievous injury was caused during the occurrence.
predicates.actor_for_grievous_injury_unidentified: The evidence does not establish which participant caused the grievous injury.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns group-assault convictions, an accused’s individual act of causing simple hurt is proved, and the cause of a grievous injury is unidentified, the conviction is limited to the proven simple hurt.
